I am 68 years old, and I have worked this land in Quzhou County since I was a girl. I never went to school, but the fields have been my teacher for fifty years. My farm is 15.5 mu—small, but it is enough for me and the one other person in my household. I draw water from my own well, so I can irrigate when the rains fail, though I am careful not to waste it because pumping costs money and strength.

This year, I will do what has always fed us and brought cash to the house. Chinese cabbage is the heart of my farm; it stores through the winter and the buyers at the market know my produce. I will put the biggest piece of land, 5 mu, into Chinese cabbage, planting in late summer for an autumn harvest. I will set aside 3 mu for regular cabbage in the spring, because it comes to market early when prices are good. Chili peppers earn well but need constant bending and picking, so I will only grow 2.5 mu—enough to make money without breaking my back, and I will hire a few days of help for the harvest. Cotton is 3 mu; it does not need as much daily fussing, and the state purchasing station takes it reliably. The last 2 mu will go to summer maize, mainly to feed us and the few animals we keep.

For seed, I save my own chili seeds from the best plants, because they are hardy and taste right for this soil. For the cabbages, I buy improved seeds from the village supply shop—hybrids are too expensive for my taste, and the improved ones do fine. But for maize, I buy hybrid seed; the old varieties disappeared years ago and nothing else yields enough to bother with. I will fertilize by watching the leaves: the cabbages are greedy, so they get the most nitrogen and potash; cotton and maize need less. I till with the rotary machine from the cooperative—it is fast and easier on my old arms than a plough. I spray pesticides only when I see aphids, worms, or leaf spots; I do not spray blindly. If the weather holds fair, I expect decent yields.
